title: Discovery: Redwood cost/unit economics discussion with Skyline AI
summary: Initial discovery focused on per-token economics, batching/caching levers, hosted vs dedicated vs private cost tradeoffs, and Skyline's budget constraints and latency SLOs. Agreed to run a short benchmark and share detailed pricing + security docs.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hi everyone thanks for joining, i'm Jordan from Redwood. we got Priya from SE as well. how's it going?
[00:07] Carlos Mendes: Hey Jordan, hey Priya. good afternoon. we (we're) excited to dig in on cost, we've been running some in-house evals and wanted to understand unit economics across hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[00:15] Priya Narang: great. quick agenda — capture current stack, traffic profile, latency SLOs, budget constraints, and then map levers: batching, kv/prefix caching, quantization, and reserved capacity. sound ok?
[00:26] Carlos Mendes: yeah perfect.
[00:29] Aisha Khan: quick note: Michael from finance is on — we want to understand predictable costs, and whether reserved capacity makes sense compared to hosted.
[00:36] Michael Park: hi all. for context we have a mid-sized LLM usage: about 4 million tokens/day across inference (mix of chat completions and embeddings), 95th p99 latency target for chat under 300ms, and monthly infra budget target of about $35k.
[00:52] Jordan Lee: ok that's super helpful. quick question on traffic shape — is that steady or spiky?
[00:56] Carlos Mendes: fairly spiky, mornings peak in US, but we do some heavy batch jobs at night for re-ranking and embeddings.
[01:05] Priya Narang: perfect — that kind of pattern benefits from burst/burstback and autoscale if you need it. on per-token pricing — hosted generally is usage-based (per-token), dedicated is usually a committed monthly cost that amortizes to a per-token equivalent depending on utilization, and private has both platform license and infra costs.
[01:24] Michael Park: can you give ballpark numbers? we've run into wildly different quoted prices across vendors.
[01:28] Jordan Lee: sure. i'll caveat: these are example numbers and we'll send formal sheet after. for hosted — our published rate for the open Llama-class models is around $0.0008 to $0.002 per input+output token depending on model and throughput; for larger models or lower-latency variants it's higher. for Dedicated, customers typically reserve a pool (eg N GPUs) — that might look like $Xk/month for the pool. amortized per-token can get to $0.0003-$0.001 depending on utilization and model size. Private has higher fixed costs — licensing + infra + ops, so per-token equivalent often depends heavily on utilization and cluster efficiency.
[02:06] Aisha Khan: that range is broad. what are the knobs to push cost down? batching? caching? quantization?
[02:12] Priya Narang: yes those are the main levers. batching increases GPU throughput by combining requests — it's great for throughput but can add latency. we support adaptive batching with SLO-aware policies. kv/prefix caching is huge for chat workloads where prompts share history — by caching the KV cache for a prefix or frequently used system prompts you avoid redoing expensive compute for the same tokens. quantization (like int8 or mixed) reduces memory and can boost throughput but can impact model quality slightly; we provide recommended profiles per model and workload.
[02:45] Carlos Mendes: can you quantify caching? like percent savings we might expect?
[02:48] Priya Narang: depends on hit rate. for chat sessions with high prefix reuse, we often see 30-60% token savings on downstream generations because the KV cache only needs to be loaded not recomputed. for templates and system prompts reused across users it can be even higher. for embeddings workflows caching isn't usually applicable.
[03:06] Jordan Lee: another nuance — batching and cache interact. if your batch aggregator sees many requests that share prefixes, we can preserve cache benefits while batching, but if batching groups unrelated requests you might pay extra latency without cache hits.
[03:18] Michael Park: you mentioned latency SLO — our target p99 300ms. is that realistic with batching and caching?
[03:23] Priya Narang: yes, with adaptive batching tuned to the SLO and using warm caches, we've seen p99 sub-300ms for Llama-2-base-ish models on dedicated pools; for very large models or cold caches it's more challenging. hosted endpoints in our regions can meet p95 easily; p99 depends on cold-starts and multi-tenant tail. Dedicated reduces variability.
[03:46] Aisha Khan: what about reserved capacity — what's the break-even on utilization? we don't want to overcommit.
[03:51] Jordan Lee: typical rule of thumb: if you can sustain 60-70% utilization of a dedicated pool, reserved is often cheaper than hosted. below ~40% hosted is often cheaper. there's a middle band where burstable dedicated or hybrid routing makes sense — keep a small reserved pool + hosted overflow.
[04:08] Carlos Mendes: ok, our traffic peaks hit ~8x baseline in mornings; sounds like hybrid might be interesting. how do you handle overflow routing?
[04:15] Priya Narang: Smart routing — policy-based. route by latency, cost, region, and customer tier. we can set rules: prefer dedicated pool for production requests under SLO, fallback to hosted for spikes, or send non-latency-sensitive batch jobs to cheaper quantized variants.
[04:31] Carlos Mendes: are there tooling / dashboards to see per-token cost?
[04:34] Jordan Lee: yes Redwood Console exposes token-level cost breakdowns, per-route cost, and per-model. you can also trace tokens to specific requests and see the amortized cost when using caching/batching.
[04:44] Michael Park: curious about security: for private do you support KMS and HSM? we have strict encryption and audit requirements.
[04:50] Priya Narang: absolutely — private deployments integrate with customer KMS, HSM options, full audit logs, SOC2 reports, and RBAC/SSO integrations. for dedicated we also support VPC peering and customer-managed keys depending on config. we'll share our security whitepaper after.
[05:04] Aisha Khan: can you share an example benchmark? like our workload: average prompt length 120 tokens, average completion 60 tokens, 4M tokens/day. what would hosted cost look like roughly?
[05:14] Jordan Lee: rough calc: 4M tokens/day * 30 days = 120M tokens/month. at $0.001 per token (mid-range hosted) that's $120k/month, so above your $35k target. but that's a naive calc — caching and batching can lower effective bill. if you get a 40% effective token saving from caching and batching, that reduces billed tokens to ~72M -> $72k/month. dedicated with good utilization could amortize to $0.0004/token -> $48k/month, closer but still above $35k. these are illustrative.
[05:46] Carlos Mendes: ok so we need to optimize prompts and invest in caching. any quick wins?
[05:50] Priya Narang: yes — prompt compression (templating), reducing unnecessary context, using system prompts sparingly, enabling prefix KV caching for chat, and using quantized model variants for non-critical requests. also rerouting low-priority bulk jobs to cheaper GPU/quantized instances.
[06:05] Michael Park: what about embeddings costs? we have nightly batch of 300k texts — any tips?
[06:09] Priya Narang: for embeddings, batch processing at night with larger batch sizes is efficient; use dedicated capacity for embeddings if volume is high. also use sharding and model quantization where supported. we can recommend a config.
[06:20] Carlos Mendes: any common transcription/ops gotchas? we've seen vendors charge per 'tokenized' vs per 'raw' token, or counts differ.
[06:27] Jordan Lee: yes, token counting differences matter; we publish our tokenization rules and provide tokenization endpoints so you can estimate. also consider cost attribution: some customers want per-feature cost split, which we support in Console.
[06:38] Aisha Khan: how long to get dedicated reserved capacity up?
[06:41] Jordan Lee: typically 2-4 weeks for provisioned pools, depending on GPU availability and enterprise contracting. private on-prem/VPC can take 6-12+ weeks depending on networking and compliance.
[06:52] Carlos Mendes: ok that's helpful. would you run a short benchmark on our workload? we can send sample prompts and historic traffic.
[06:58] Priya Narang: absolutely — next step we usually run a 7–10 day benchmark: we take a workload sample, run it on hosted and on a small dedicated pool (and optionally a quantized variant), measure latency, p95/p99, and effective tokens billed with caching/batching configured. we produce a report with amortized per-token costs.
[07:17] Michael Park: timeline on that?
[07:19] Jordan Lee: if you can share sample data by Friday we can spin up a small dedicated pool within ~10 business days and have preliminary results in about 2 weeks.
[07:29] Carlos Mendes: ok we'll share a redacted sample and a spreadsheet with traffic shape.
[07:33] Aisha Khan: any contract minimums?
[07:36] Jordan Lee: for Dedicated reserved capacity there's a minimum monthly commitment (varies by pool size) and discounts for annual commit. Hosted is self-serve. Private has licensing and setup fees. we'll include options in the pricing sheet.
[07:47] Carlos Mendes: you mentioned quality regression risks when quantizing — do you run evals?
[07:52] Priya Narang: yes our Optimize tooling runs evals on prompt sets to estimate quality delta when moving to quantized or smaller model variants. we tie regressions to alerting so you don't silently degrade UX.
[08:03] Michael Park: ok that reduces risk.
[08:05] Jordan Lee: quick recap then — action items: we'll send pricing sheet for hosted vs dedicated vs private, include break-even examples using your numbers; we'll share security whitepaper + SOC2; SE team will prepare a 7–10 day benchmark plan and a list of required artifacts; and we'll propose a hybrid routing config suggestion.
[08:23] Carlos Mendes: sounds good. one more question — competitors, do you see customers switching from OpenAI or Anthropic often for cost reasons?
[08:30] Priya Narang: yes often it's driven by cost or model governance. some customers use OpenAI for highest quality outputs; others adopt open models on Redwood for cost and control. we support routing and model fallback strategies so you can mix.
[08:43] Michael Park: great. next steps?
[08:45] Jordan Lee: we'll email the pricing + security docs and the benchmark plan by Friday. let's target a technical deep-dive once the benchmark results are in.
[08:54] Carlos Mendes: perfect thanks everyone.
[08:56] Jordan Lee: thanks all, talk soon.
[08:58] [END TRANSCRIPT]
